title: How to Order from Temu in Pakistan (Step by Step)
summary: How do you order from Temu in Pakistan? The step-by-step process, why cards get declined, customs on arrival, and the cash-on-delivery route.
body_markdown:
There is no Pakistani version of Temu. No rupee checkout, no cash on delivery, no local warehouse and no returns address in Lahore or Karachi. Ordering from here means placing a cross-border order on a foreign storefront, and it has to survive three checkpoints: Temu has to ship to your address, your card has to clear an international payment, and the parcel has to get through customs. Most Pakistani attempts fail at one of those three, usually the card. Below is the sequence in the order you will actually meet it, what to do when a step refuses you, and the cash-on-delivery route to the same Chinese products if the answer at any checkpoint is no.


## Before you start: the three checkpoints


Everything in this guide hangs off these, so check them before you spend an hour filling a cart.


1. **Serviceability.** Temu only accepts orders for countries it has set up. If Pakistan is not selectable as a delivery destination in your app, nothing below matters — no address workaround changes it.
2. **Payment.** Checkout is prepaid and in a foreign currency. Your card must be open for international transactions, and many Pakistani debit cards are not by default.
3. **Clearance.** The parcel arrives as an import. It may be assessed, and any duty is collected before it reaches you.


If you only want to know whether orders get through at all,[is Temu available in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/is-temu-available-in-pakistan) answers that on its own. This post assumes you have decided to try and want the mechanics.


## Step 1 — Set the country before you browse anything


Open the app or the site and set the delivery country first, in settings or from the region picker on the home screen. Do it before you browse. Prices, shipping options, delivery estimates and even which items appear are all destination-specific, so a cart built while the app thinks you are somewhere else is not your cart.


This is also the honest availability test. If Pakistan is not in the country list, or selecting it empties the catalogue, the app is telling you it does not serve this market. That is a product decision on Temu's side, not something you can configure around.


## Step 2 — Check the item ships to a Pakistani address


Serviceability on Temu is per item, not just per country. Open the listing and read the shipping block under the price — the one that names a delivery window for your destination. An item with no estimate for Pakistan is not orderable here, however many times it is added to the cart.


Two things that catch people out:


- **Category restrictions.** Batteries, aerosols, liquids, power banks and anything with a lithium cell are commonly restricted on cross-border air freight. A listing can be perfectly available while the same product in another size or format is not.
- **Seller-level differences.** The same product from two sellers can have two different destination lists. If one refuses your address, the other may not.


## Step 3 — Build the cart around shipping, not the sticker


The sticker price is the least interesting number on the page for a Pakistani order. What you pay is the item, plus international shipping, plus whatever customs assesses on arrival, plus the currency conversion your bank applies. Three habits keep that landed number from surprising you:


- **Consolidate.** Several small items in one order usually travel better than the same items ordered separately across a week. Separate orders mean separate parcels, separate tracking numbers and separate chances to be held.
- **Read the delivery window, not the shipping label.** Names like "standard" and "express" mean different things on a cross-border lane. The date range is the promise; the label is marketing.
- **Favour light, flat, unbreakable goods.** The categories Temu prices hardest are the ones that ship cheaply. Heavy or fragile items lose their price advantage somewhere over the Arabian Sea.


For the full breakdown of why the model produces those prices and where it stops working here, see[Temu in Pakistan: how it works, shipping and alternatives](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/temu-in-pakistan-how-it-works-shipping-alternatives) .


## Step 4 — Enter an address a Pakistani courier can actually use


The last mile is handled by a local courier, and local couriers here navigate by landmark and phone call, not by postcode. The form is built for countries where the opposite is true, so do the translation yourself:


- Put the house or shop number, street and block in address line 1, and the sector, town or nearest landmark in line 2. "Near Chandni Chowk" is worth more than any postcode.
- Write the city exactly as couriers know it, and pick the right province in the dropdown.
- Enter the phone in full international format with the country code, and use a number that will be answered by whoever is at that address.
- Use the postcode if you know it. Leave it correct rather than clever — a made-up postcode can fail validation on the carrier's side.


A wrong or unanswered phone number is the most common self-inflicted delay on any cross-border parcel into Pakistan. The courier gets one or two attempts, then the parcel sits.


## Step 5 — Pay, which is where most Pakistani orders stop


Checkout is card-first and prepaid. There is no cash on delivery, and no rupee wallet to top up. Before you reach this screen, check three things with your bank:


- **International transactions are enabled** on the card. On most Pakistani banks this is a toggle in the app, off by default, and sometimes a separate limit you have to raise.
- **The card is open for e-commerce** as well as ATM use, and the online spending limit covers the order.
- **You know which account the money leaves from** , because a failed foreign transaction can still place a hold that takes days to fall off.


If the payment is declined, the fix is with your bank, not with Temu. What you should not do is hand your card details, or your money, to someone in a Facebook group who offers to place the order for you. Paying a stranger in advance for a parcel from abroad is the single easiest way to lose the money entirely, and there is no dispute process that will get it back for you.


The prepaid-versus-COD question is the whole decision for most buyers here, and it is worked through in[Temu vs Markaz for buyers in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/temu-vs-markaz-which-is-better-for-buyers-in-pakistan) .


## Step 6 — Track it, and learn to read the silence


After payment the parcel moves through the same legs as any China-to-Pakistan shipment: the seller hands it to a consolidation warehouse in China, it waits for a load going this way, it flies or sails, it clears customs here, and a local courier delivers it.


The part that alarms first-time buyers is the quiet stretch. On consolidated services a parcel is scanned when it enters the Chinese network and again when it lands in the destination country, with little in between. A tracking page that has not moved in two weeks is usually a parcel in transit, not a lost one. The time to act is when the buyer-protection window on the order is running out, not when tracking is boring. What each leg involves, and where the days actually go, is covered in[how long China-to-Pakistan delivery takes](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/china-to-pakistan-delivery-time) .


## Step 7 — Customs, and the bill at the door


Your parcel enters Pakistan as an import. Most small consignments clear without drama, some are held for assessment, and duty and taxes may be charged on the assessed value. The courier normally collects whatever is owed before handing the parcel over.


Two consequences worth planning for. First, the number you paid at checkout is not necessarily the number the order costs you — budget for the possibility of a bill at the door. Second, if nobody is there with the money, the delivery fails and the parcel goes back to the depot. Cross-border prices are real, but they are pre-clearance prices, and the landed cost is the only figure worth comparing against a local one.


## Step 8 — If it arrives wrong


This is the weakest part of the process from Pakistan. There is no local returns address, so a return means shipping the item back across a border at a cost that can exceed what the item was worth. In practice buyers here do one of three things: claim within the platform's buyer-protection window and argue it out in the app, keep the item and absorb the loss, or give up.


What improves your odds: photograph the parcel before you open it and the item immediately after, keep the packaging, and raise the claim inside the window rather than waiting to see if you can live with the fault. Order small the first time, from a seller with a long review history, and treat the first order as a test of the route rather than a purchase you are depending on.


## What the process really costs you


Add the steps up and the trade is clear enough. You get close-to-source prices on light goods, and you pay for them with a prepaid card, a wait measured in weeks, a customs bill you cannot price in advance, and effectively no returns. For a cheap phone case that is a fine deal. For anything you need by a date, or anything that has to fit, or anything you are buying to resell, the risk sits in the wrong place — with you, before the product has proved it works.


That calculation is the same one behind every cross-border platform serving this market, which is why it is worth reading the wider map of[online shopping in Pakistan](https://www.markaz.app/blog-post/cheapest-online-shopping-in-pakistan) before committing to any one route. Everything above gets heavier when the parcel is stock rather than a purchase. Prepaying ties your money up for the whole shipping window before you know the product sells. A customs bill you did not forecast eats the margin you were counting on. A faulty batch has to go back to China at your cost, and your customer is waiting the whole time.

## Frequently asked questions


### Can I order from Temu in Pakistan at all?


Sometimes, and not reliably. Temu is not set up for this market the way it is for the countries it operates in properly: no rupee checkout, no cash on delivery, no local stock and no returns address here. Whether a given order goes through depends on whether your address is serviceable and whether your card clears an international payment.


### Does Temu offer cash on delivery in Pakistan?


No. Checkout is prepaid by card. For Chinese products with cash on delivery in rupees, Markaz China is the route Pakistani buyers use instead.


### Why is my card being declined on Temu?


Nearly always because international transactions are not enabled on the card, the online spending limit is too low, or the card is not open for e-commerce use. All three are settings on your bank's side — fix them in your banking app or by calling the bank, then retry.


### How long does a Temu parcel take to reach Pakistan?


Weeks rather than days, because the parcel travels as a cross-border consignment and then clears customs before a local courier delivers it. The estimate shown at checkout after you set Pakistan as the destination is the only one specific to your order.


### Will I pay customs duty on a Temu order?


You can. Parcels entering Pakistan may be assessed and the courier usually collects before delivering. Treat the checkout total as a pre-clearance price and budget for the possibility of a bill at the door.


### Can I return a Temu item from Pakistan?


Not easily. There is no local returns address, so sending an item back means paying international shipping that can cost more than the item. Raise a claim inside the platform's buyer-protection window instead, with photos taken when the parcel arrived.


### Is it safe to let someone else order for me?


Paying a stranger to place an order on your behalf, or giving out your card details, is the most common way people lose money on this route. If your own card will not clear, use a platform that accepts payment at the door rather than routing the purchase through a third party.


### Is Temu worth it for resellers in Pakistan?


As a supply chain it is awkward: prepaid, slow, unpredictable at customs, and hard to return. Fine for buying one sample to look at. Poor for stock your customers are waiting on.
